/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.headline: Flashbulbs, lies and victim blaming: how Russell Brand’s trial unfolded
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.excerpt: Russell Brand’s trial at Southwark crown court, which ended with him being found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others, was one of the most obsessively watched criminal cases in recent history. As well as Brand’s own conduct, the case became an examination of his victims’ evidence, the legal strategy his team used to defend him, and the culture within which he committed his crimes. The victims: ‘I remember him on me. I know I said no’ Brand’s victims told how he “snapped” from charming to nasty as he raped and sexually assaulted them before gaslighting them into believing nothing was wrong. The comedian’s youngest victim, who was 21 when he targeted her at the height of his fame in 2009, was left traumatised by their encounter. Brand had stored her name in his phone alongside a series of letters and symbols. The court heard the letter “T” stood for “tart”, while “AP” denoted anal play, and two asterisks meant: “Never, ever forget this individual, this is a memorable encounter.” It was, indeed, an encounter the woman would never forget, she spent years torturing and blaming herself for what happened. The woman was starstruck when she met Brand after one of his standup performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009. Brand, who was more than a decade her senior, picked the woman from the crowd and invited her to his dressing room. There, she performed oral sex on him and engaged in a threesome with another young fan.
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.trail: Level of interest in comedian’s case resulted in examination of affairs inside and outside the courtroom

/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.headline: Russell Brand faces ‘significant’ prison term for rape and sexual assault
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.excerpt: Russell Brand has been found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three other women, ending a years-long legal saga that has raised questions about how he was able to commit his crimes at the height of his fame. Brand, 51, was described during his trial as a ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator. He was convicted of raping a woman at his luxury London townhouse and of sexually assaulting women in front of his entourage at their workplaces, at a radio station and TV studio. The Hollywood actor turned online influencer was accused of gaslighting his victims after the attacks, and treating women as a “disposable commodity” and a “means to an end” to satisfy his voracious sexual appetite. It can now be revealed that Brand is under investigation for two further rape allegations and that the Metropolitan police have submitted files to the Crown Prosecution Service. Brand – who will be sentenced on Monday – stood outside the door of the dock shortly before the jury delivered their verdicts and looked at his wife, Laura, saying: “Laura, I love you.” Wearing a grey three-piece suit, he appeared to be praying in the dock before he was convicted of four offences on Thursday after a four-week trial at Southwark crown court. He had pleaded not guilty to three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999.
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.trail: Actor and comedian, 51, found guilty of raping a woman and assaulting three others

/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.headline: Misogyny and sexism of Russell Brand case have not gone away, TV insiders say
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.excerpt: Even within the culture of casual misogyny and sexism that pervaded the TV world in the mid-noughties, Naomi Harvey and her colleagues concluded they needed to do something about Russell Brand. Harvey was one of a team of researchers tasked with finding fans of Big Brother, Channel 4’s reality TV juggernaut, to appear on the discussion show Big Brother’s Big Mouth, hosted by Brand. They had noticed Brand’s habit of asking a runner, the most junior person on the production, to obtain the phone numbers of female audience members and pass them to him. But something new had just happened. A distraught audience member had phoned Harvey to complain after being invited for drinks by Brand after the show. “All I remember is being really taken aback that she was so upset,” Harvey recalled. “We noticed this behaviour of taking women’s numbers, and now it had escalated to the point that we’d had a member of the public phone up the desk upset. “We felt as the audience team we had a responsibility, so me and my two colleagues reported it up to our next boss. “We never heard anything again.” The episode is minor when set against the criminality exposed during Brand’s trial. Yet it is part of a culture that appeared to indulge Brand and fail to confront troubling behaviour. Brand’s case has led to difficult questions for the BBC, Channel 4 and the production companies that worked with him.
/culture/2026/nov/06/russell-brand-trial.trail: Concerns remain that media industry is still failing to confront troubling behaviour

/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.headline: US carries out another round of ‘minor’ strikes on Iran, Trump says
/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.excerpt: Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.” Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February. In an exchange with reporters on Friday, Trump said “they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five”. The US military had previously reported carrying out what it described as “defensive” strikes on Monday, when explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas. Friday’s strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US. The electoral setback was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s execution of the Iran war and elevated fuel prices – a byproduct of the war that has affected nearly every part of the global economy. In the days since, Trump has vacillated between threatening to “destroy” Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near. Differences with Iran about its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.
/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.trail: The president’s announcement comes days after an earlier attack on Iran was made public, and as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have accelerated

/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.headline: How Stephen Miller appointment shows Trump hasn’t learned his lesson on immigration
/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.excerpt: On Tuesday, voters resoundingly rebuked Donald Trump and his brutal mass deportation campaign that sent military tanks and masked agents though residential streets. But on Friday, the president doubled down. He named Stephen Miller – the architect of the administration’s most aggressive immigration policies – as his chief of staff. It was never likely that Trump – who rose to political prominence on the promise that he would expel immigrants en masse from the US – would dampen his agenda, even after voters rejected Republican candidates up and down the ballot, near and far from the southern border, in blue and deep-red states. But the elevation of Miller – a zealous, anti-immigrant crusader who has been by Trump’s side since the president’s first term – is an ominous signal that the deportation machine that Trump has built up over the past two years will be driving ahead at full speed. Miller more than any single other person is responsible for unleashing a series of violent immigration raids across US cities this year and last, for sending hordes of masked agents in military gear through residential streets to round up undocumented immigrants. He has pushed the administration to all but shut down legal immigration as well. In his previous roles – as a deputy chief of staff and policy adviser – he has stuck close to Trump’s side and stoked the president’s most extreme instincts.
/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.trail: US voters repudiated mass deportation campaign, but choice of new chief of staff shows Trump doesn’t care

/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.headline: Susie Wiles exits White House as Trump ousts another woman from key role
/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.excerpt: Donald Trump on Friday said Susie Wiles, the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, will leave her post, a major shake-up of his inner circle that comes amid a steady exodus of senior female officials from his administration. The president announced her ouster – and her replacement, by the immigration hardliner Stephen Miller – in a post on Truth Social, days after a sweeping blue wave gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections. Wiles’s departure leaves behind an overwhelmingly male leadership team. “I wanted to make a change,” he told reporters on Friday. “I think Susie’s done a very good job … Stephen’s been great and we’ve got to make moves.” Wiles, who reportedly handed in her resignation on Thursday night, said her role as chief of staff “has been the honor of a lifetime,” adding: “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together, from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America first.” Wiles’s exit follows a string of high-profile resignations and dismissals of women in the Trump administration. In recent months, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was ousted just five days after taking up the role, while former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem and former attorney general Pam Bondi were also dismissed.
/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.trail: Wiles thanks president for ‘honor of a lifetime’ as departure leaves behind overwhelmingly male leadership team

/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.headline: Two more DoJ officials resign, including US attorney leading inquiry into Trump rivals
/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.excerpt: A US attorney overseeing the so-called “grand conspiracy” investigation into Donald Trump’s rivals announced on Friday he is leaving the Department of Justice, one of several officials to leave the department in recent days after sweeping Democratic wins in the midterm elections. Jason Reding Quiñones, the US attorney for the southern district of Florida, and John Eisenberg, who led the justice department’s national security division, are both leaving. Democrats have pledged to use their majorities in the US House and Senate to conduct aggressive oversight of the justice department, among other agencies. Quiñones had been overseeing an inquiry into whether former top government officials engaged in a “grand conspiracy” to violate Trump’s rights when they investigated him after the 2020 election. Conservative allies had high hopes for the investigation, whose targets included the former CIA director John Brennan, among others. But there were personnel issues and charges have not yet been filed. “The ‘grand conspiracy’ case into the lawfare against the president is essentially dead now,” Julie Kelly, a conservative commentator, posted on X. “We are grateful for Jason’s leadership in combating violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking and transnational crime, including the indictment of Raúl Castro,” the US attorney general, Todd Blanche, said in a statement. Eisenberg led the national security division, which oversees terrorism and espionage cases, among others.
/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.trail: Jason Reding Quiñones led investigation into whether Trump’s rights were violated during 2020 election inquiry

/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.headline: Trump will be blocked from putting ‘rightwinger’ on supreme court, Schumer says
/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.excerpt: Donald Trump will be blocked from putting a “rightwinger” on the US supreme court, according to Chuck Schumer, the soon-to-be Senate majority leader, in remarks that were a preview of how Democrats intend to wield their power come January. In an interview with the Associated Press, Schumer said Democrats would not confirm “any crappy nominees” to the supreme court, lower courts or Trump’s cabinet. “The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a rightwinger on the court,” Schumer said. Four supreme court justices are in their 70s, and its two most conservative justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, are the oldest on the court at 78 and 76 years old, respectively. After scoring massive midterm-election wins and taking back both chambers of Congress, Democratic leaders are planning their comeback for when the new Congress is sworn in. That includes major pushback against the US president and his policies. Some Democrats are planning to launch investigations into Trump and members of his administration. On Tuesday evening, Robert Garcia, the soon-to-be chair of the House oversight committee, warned Republicans to “lawyer up”. Others are preparing to push forward legislation they promised to voters, and Democratic leaders will enjoy wide margins in both the House and Senate to pass key priorities like restoring Medicaid cuts from Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and halting funding for the war in Iran. Trump has indicated he plans to veto bills he doesn’t agree with.
/us-news/2026/nov/06/stephen-miller-chie.trail: After midterm wins, Democratics plan comeback for when new Congress is sworn in, including pushback against Trump and his policies

/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.headline: US tech stocks recover after selloff spooks investors over AI spending
/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.excerpt: US tech stocks made a recovery on Tuesday afternoon after a selloff spooked investors over AI spending. Tuesday’s midterm elections didn’t appear to have a huge impact on Wall Street, though investors are predicting Democrats get at least a majority in the House and potentially gain seats in the Senate, which could lead to more AI regulation. The S&P 500 was up 0.37% at market closing on Tuesday, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq increased 0.83% for the day. The Dow dropped 0.38% following a 1.9% dip in Apple’s share price after the company released a worse-than-expected margin forecast due to the higher cost of memory chips. Nvidia picked up a 2.3% gain after dropping over four sessions, while fellow chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom and Micron Technology also jumped on Tuesday. Tuesday marked the end of a brief selloff of AI and tech stocks that started last week, with the Nasdaq in October experiencing its largest monthly decline since March 2025. The Nasdaq had ended on Monday in correction territory, dropping 10% from its 6 October record close. Small drops in oil prices, amid potential new negotiations with Iran and Russia, also eased investors. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, dropped to $103 a barrel on Tuesday, down from $117 a barrel at the end of October.
/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.trail: Midterms didn’t appear to have huge impact, though predicted wins for Democrats could mean more regulation

/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.headline: Tech sell-off drives US markets down by nearly $1tn after subpar earnings reports
/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.excerpt: A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies drove US markets down by hundreds of billions of dollars on Friday. In total, the decline has knocked nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month. The S&P 500, the index of the 500 most valuable companies in the US, fell by more than 1% Friday, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. It was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the same month. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down even further, more than 3%, also erasing hundreds of billions in value. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell less. More than $2tn in market value is set to be wiped from the Nasdaq ⁠100 this month, as big tech earnings intensified investor scrutiny of whether the billions being poured into artificial intelligence can generate returns quickly enough. The wipeout would amount to slightly more than SpaceX’s entire market value. ⁠The index has fallen ⁠more than 5.8% so far in October as the AI trade ran into turbulence, with hyperscalers Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Amazon raising spending forecasts further as they race to expand AI infrastructure. Intel tumbled nearly 30% and is flirting with its worst day since 1974, even though the chipmaker reported stronger profits for the latest quarter than analysts expected.
/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.trail: Big tech stocks falter as investors question whether billions being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enough

/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.headline: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll
/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.excerpt: Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector. The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period. The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg. AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market. The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market. The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit. The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.
/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.trail: Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom

/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.headline: Meta plans $95bn stock offering to help cover AI expansion
/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.excerpt: Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta has announced plans for $95bn (£71bn) of fundraising to cover its AI expenditure, even as Elon Musk warned that funding for smaller players in the sector was drying up. The owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp is a leading investor in AI and is ploughing multibillion-dollar sums into datacentres, the central nervous systems of the technology. Meta’s announcement on Monday came after Musk added to the pressure on “neocloud” datacentre providers – which lease computing power to AI companies – by saying the sector faced “death and consolidation” amid concerns over the sustainability of their funding. The Meta fundraising will come in two parts. In the first, the company plans to raise $35bn through new “underwritten public offerings” – a sale of company stock. This has some big-name backers, with chipmakers Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom all showing interest, Meta said. These “cornerstone investors” could buy up to $5bn of the stock on offer. In the second, Meta also plans to launch a $60bn “at-the-market offering” to sell new common stock to investors at the going market rate in future. That offering involves selling Meta’s new class C stock, which it announced it was creating last week. These class C shares do not have voting rights, so can be sold without diluting Zuckerberg’s control of the company. The Silicon Valley company said these plans would support “Meta’s continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence”.
/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.trail: Tech firm announces two-part fundraising after Elon Musk warns hundreds of AI startups face collapse

/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.headline: Anthropic files for potentially record-breaking stock market valuation in key test for AI industry
/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.excerpt: Anthropic has publicly filed for a stock market listing in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company’s float on the US market will serve as a test of the financial viability of the multitrillion-dollar AI boom. Analysts and investors have valued the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, at more than $1.5tn. The company, which will will list under the symbol ANT, confidentially filed with US financial regulators for an initial public offering in June. “We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history,” the company’s investor prospectus reads. Anthropic researchers and executives have trumpeted the transformative power of AI while simultaneously warning of its potential to cause human extinction. A leader in the race to create powerful artificial intelligence models and a bellwether of the American AI boom, Anthropic’s chatbot Claude is its flagship product, which offers text generation features as well as advanced coding and cybersecurity capabilities. CEO Dario Amodei founded the company after quitting OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT. Anthropic’s audited filings will offer the first public glimpse of its financial health, which have been the object of intense speculation in recent months as questions of a potential AI bubble swirl.
/business/2026/nov/06/global-stocks-plun.trail: Market debut of firm behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of AI boom’s financial viability

/world/2026/nov/06/boy-six-third-in-chil.headline: Why have more than 30 European flights been hit by bomb threats this week?
/world/2026/nov/06/boy-six-third-in-chil.excerpt: More than 30 planes have been subjected to security alerts or diversions this week, with at least 25 more bomb threats on Thursday disrupting civil aviation across Europe. What do we know so far, and how concerned should you be about your travel plans? What’s happened? At least 34 flights have been disrupted this week, beginning on Monday, when a Wizz Air flight from London Luton to Sofia in Bulgaria was diverted to Budapest. Thursday’s threats affected airports in London, Birmingham, Brussels, Bucharest, Madrid, Milan, Prague, Rome, Sofia and Warsaw, among others. So far all incidents have been confirmed to be false alarms, with nothing suspicious found by relevant security authorities. Which airports and airlines have been most affected? There is no clear pattern of airports and airlines targeted, although a significant number have involved Italian airports as an origin or destination. Seven flights this week were to – or from the UK – and four to or from Ireland. Sofia and Milan each recorded six incidents, followed by Rome (five) and Prague (four). Ryanair was the hardest-hit airline, with eight reported cases. The EU transport commissioner, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, said on Thursday it was “too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked”. He stressed: “Any threats against civilians are unacceptable.” Who is behind these threats?
/world/2026/nov/06/boy-six-third-in-chil.trail: With flights disrupted, how concerned should you be about your travel plans?

/world/2026/nov/06/boy-six-third-in-chil.headline: Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?
/world/2026/nov/06/boy-six-third-in-chil.excerpt: Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries have malfunctioned, their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F). The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”. Which supermarkets were affected and what does it mean? The attack hit fridges in Belgian branches of Carrefour, Intermarché and Ikea, Coop and ICA in Sweden, Delhaize in Luxembourg, Kesko in Finland, SuperValu in Ireland and shops in Estonia. It appeared to be a reprise of attacks three weeks ago when French retailers had to ditch huge amounts of food when their fridges suddenly overheated as a result of anonymous hackers seizing control of their internet-exposed appliance management software. Something similar may have happened in the US in early August when a series of mysterious fridge malfunctions hit commissaries at least six military bases. The Pentagon is investigating a suspected hack. This is feared to signal a new front in cyber-attack and hacking tactics. Fridges are not unique in having their controls exposed to hackers. Many ovens, washing machines, dishwashers and central heating systems are linked to the internet to allow remote access and automated control. Who is doing it?
/world/2026/nov/06/boy-six-third-in-chil.trail: After a second apparent cyber-attack in weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motives

/world/2026/nov/06/boy-six-third-in-chil.headline: Ryanair faces clash with unions as it mulls pay freezes amid soaring fuel costs
/world/2026/nov/06/boy-six-third-in-chil.excerpt: Ryanair has said it is considering implementing pay freezes, setting the scene for a confrontation with unions as the airline tries to offset soaring fuel costs driven by the Middle East conflict. The airline is also considering reducing crew numbers on flights and increasing the use of AI, in a cost-cutting drive. Europe’s largest low-cost carrier said it expected European airlines to raise ticket prices by up to 20%, with its own jet fuel costs forecast to rise by about €2bn (£1.6bn) in its next financial year, which ends in March 2028. “Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict we expect jet fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027,” said Michael O’Leary, the chief executive of Ryanair. “While we believe European short-haul fares will increase materially to reflect these much higher jet-fuel prices and competitor capacity reductions, this is unlikely to provide a full offset for an estimated €2bn increase in our fuel bill.” Oil prices hit a six-month high on Friday before falling to about $106 a barrel on Monday. Ryanair expects European short-haul fares to “increase materially” next year, as fuel hedging deals taken out by airlines to reduce costs expire. “To help address this, we’re reviewing all costs across group airlines with a particular focus on airport churn negotiations, maturing labour agreements (which may require temporary pay freezes), lower crew ratios and increased use of AI,” O’Leary said.
/world/2026/nov/06/boy-six-third-in-chil.trail: Airline also weighs up reducing crew on flights and increasing use of AI as part of cost-cutting measures

/world/2026/nov/06/boy-six-third-in-chil.headline: Union in plea to save Poundland from administration, with 12,000 jobs at risk
/world/2026/nov/06/boy-six-third-in-chil.excerpt: The shop workers’ union Usdaw has urged Poundland’s owners to reconsider a decision to prepare the budget chain for administration, putting up to 12,000 jobs at risk. Gordon Brothers filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators to Poundland at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process. The legal measure protects Poundland from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought. Gordon Brothers previously rejected a management-backed rescue bid for the discount chain, which operates 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland. It bought the struggling chain for a nominal £1 from its previous owner, the European retail group Pepco, in June 2025. Only one bidder, Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish family-owned company, was interested in buying the entire chain and working with the existing management, led by Barry Williams, the chief executive. Gordon Brothers is understood to believe that it can raise more from a breakup of Poundland than through the Martin offer, which was worth less than the £30m in debts that Gordon Brothers took on when it bought the chain. The threat of administration leaves thousands of shop workers facing uncertainty in the run-up to Christmas. Rival cut-price retailers, including Poundstretcher, The Range and B&M, have reportedly expressed an interest in taking on some Poundland stores.
/world/2026/nov/06/boy-six-third-in-chil.trail: Gordon Brothers files notice of intent to begin process after rejecting management-backed rescue bid

/world/2026/nov/06/boy-six-third-in-chil.excerpt: The Long Wave is two! And over the past year, once again, it has surprised us with the breadth of stories and events in the diaspora. /uk-news/2026/nov/06/prince-harry-others.headline: Prince Harry and others ordered to pay interim £9.5m to Daily Mail publisher
/uk-news/2026/nov/06/prince-harry-others.excerpt: The Duke of Sussex and six other high-profile claimants must make a £9.54m interim payment within seven days towards the Daily Mail publisher’s legal costs after losing their high court case over allegations of unlawful information gathering, a judge has ruled. Associated Newspapers Ltd strongly denied the claims made by Prince Harry and co-claimants including Doreen Lawrence and Elton John. Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed all the claims last month after an 11-week trial in London earlier this year. The court had been told that ANL’s legal costs were £34.5m. Lawyers for the claimants, who also include John’s husband, David Furnish, the actors Sadie Frost and Liz Hurley and the former Liberal Democrat minister Simon Hughes, had argued the interim payment should be just over £7.9m. The £9.54m must be paid by 4pm on 28 August. In the costs ruling on Friday, Nicklin also said that, aside from where orders had already been made, ANL’s costs should be determined on an indemnity basis. This means that, as the losing party, the prince and the others must pay towards ANL’s costs without the publisher needing to show these were proportionate. An indemnity basis is more unusual than a standard basis, and there must be conduct or circumstances “outside of the norm”.
/uk-news/2026/nov/06/prince-harry-others.trail: Judge orders payment within seven days towards legal costs in failed case over alleged unlawful information gathering

/music/2026/nov/06/macklemore-arenas-fre.headline: Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour review – a triumph of a show with performances from Hozier, Kneecap and more
/music/2026/nov/06/macklemore-arenas-fre.excerpt: “We’d like to thank Ed Sheeran for organising this concert,” offers a member of Kneecap, one of several unannounced guests who have turned up for the first European date of Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour. It’s a characteristically two-fisted approach to the matter in hand from a band who have seldom shied away from controversy, but it has more than a grain of truth in it. The events of the last six weeks are quite something, and perhaps not what Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots, had in mind when he led efforts to pressurise Sheeran to remove Macklemore from his summer US tour, after the rapper made a speech about Palestine on stage at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium. Macklemore was duly removed from the tour, but the rapper saw his profile rise dramatically as a result – in fairness, he was hardly unknown, but his biggest hits are a decade old – while every other artist on Sheeran’s tour quit in solidarity. Sheeran’s tour limped on amid much opprobrium, while Macklemore was able to translate the publicity into a tour of his own, in noticeably bigger venues than he played on his last European tour, with proceeds donated to organisations assisting Palestinians. Dublin’s 13,000-capacity 3Arena is sold out, as is every other date on the tour.

/music/2026/nov/06/macklemore-arenas-fre.headline: Ed Sheeran’s concerts in Massachusetts canceled due to severe weather
/music/2026/nov/06/macklemore-arenas-fre.excerpt: Ed Sheeran’s concerts at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, have been canceled due to severe weather, adding further complication to a tour embroiled in controversy. On Friday, Sheeran’s tour promoter, Messina Touring, said: “Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium.” “The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority,” Messina Touring added. Sheeran had been scheduled to perform at the 64,628-seat arena on Friday and Saturday as part of his Loop tour. The cancellations come after weeks of controversy surrounding the tour, after efforts by the stadium’s billionaire owner, Robert Kraft, to rally other stadium owners and pressure Sheeran to remove Macklemore from his tour’s opening acts after the rapper called for a “free Palestine” at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Macklemore’s comments, including, “‘Free Palestine!’ I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them,” drew the ire of pro-Israel organizations, which accused the singer of “ambushing” fans with “anti-Israel propaganda”.

/music/2026/nov/06/macklemore-arenas-fre.headline: Charlotte Church accuses Ed Sheeran of ‘choosing capitalism over doing the right thing’
/music/2026/nov/06/macklemore-arenas-fre.excerpt: Charlotte Church has accused Ed Sheeran of choosing “consumerism and capitalism over doing the right thing” over the removal of his friend and support act Macklemore from his US tour. Sheeran’s tour was thrown into crisis after Macklemore made “free Palestine” declarations on stage. After a significant backlash, including pressure from the owners of stadiums hosting scheduled shows, the rapper was removed from the tour. Shortly afterwards, Sheeran’s other support acts quit in solidarity. Sheeran addressed the controversy during his concert in Philadelphia on Saturday, saying what was happening in Gaza was “catastrophic and unjustifiable”. He apologised to fans, saying: “I’ve had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I’m so, so sorry.” He added that he wanted his music and shows to be about unity and humanity, not politics. Church, who has previously been vocal about her support for Palestinians, said: “Ed Sheeran, we’re watching you,” during a gig in Cardiff on Sunday, and urged the audience to chant “free Palestine”. She said: “Whilst he [Sheeran] has made millions and has an enormous following – he has an enormous platform to do real good in the world – he chose consumerism and capitalism over doing the right thing. “So we say the same thing to Ed Sheeran because fuck the fact that musicians shouldn’t be involved in politics. Fuck that shit.

/technology/2026/nov/06/struggling-to-sp.headline: iPhone Duo owners report cracks in Apple’s first foldable handset
/technology/2026/nov/06/struggling-to-sp.excerpt: Owners of the new foldable iPhone are reporting cracks in the device’s screen, as Apple confirmed an issue with a “small number” of units. Reports of cracks have emerged on Reddit and social media platforms since the handset went on general sale globally on Friday. Experts said there had been too few examples to determine whether there was a more serious problem with Apple’s first foldable device, which retails from $1,999 (£1,499). Apple confirmed some devices had been affected by a display glitch. “We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement,” it said. One user in Australia reported that their Duo had cracked within six hours of taking ownership of it and posted their experience on Reddit. “I was showing it to a friend, and as I opened it, I felt something around the internal hinge, underneath the screen,” they wrote alongside an image of the phone showing an apparent display malfunction where a white strip of light ran along one half of the screen. “As I continued opening it, I heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge.” They said their local Apple store had replaced the phone immediately. The Guardian has been unable to verify the user’s claims. Another user in Australia posted that they had heard “almost a cracking noise” on their handset, which resulted in a similar screen malfunction.

/technology/2026/nov/06/struggling-to-sp.headline: iPhone 18 Pro Max review: Apple’s biggest, heaviest and longest-lasting superphone
/technology/2026/nov/06/struggling-to-sp.excerpt: Apple’s largest Pro iPhone gets its biggest battery upgrade yet to make it a true two-day phone with new Siri AI and a variable aperture camera. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the supersized sibling of the regular 18 Pro and, though it is no longer Apple’s most expensive phone thanks to the £2,000 iPhone Duo, it has a similarly large price tag to match costing from £1,299 (€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299). The 18 Pro Max follows the familiar formula of its Pro Max predecessors: take everything that’s great about the 18 Pro and supersize the screen and the battery. That means it has a first-class camera, the fastest performance and very long software support. But it also means the 18 Pro Max is hard to use with one hand and pretty big to fit in a pocket. It weighs 249g, which is really heavy for even a very large smartphone, 23g more than its nearest rival, 38g more than its smaller sibling and heavier still than folding phones. It made my hand hurt after 10 days of use and is a two-handed phone needing some sort of handle or strap. The 6.9in screen is a joy to behold. Super bright, crisp, smooth and with a very effective anti-glare coating it’s great for films, TV or games, and offers a similar level of real estate for video to most folding phones. It also has the new, smaller camera cut out and bigger dynamic island of the regular 18 Pro.
/technology/2026/nov/06/struggling-to-sp.trail: A giant screen, big battery, rapid chip and top cameras push the great iPhone 18 Pro to the max with a price tag to match

/technology/2026/nov/06/struggling-to-sp.headline: Apple iPhone 18 Pro review: big changes for small differences
/technology/2026/nov/06/struggling-to-sp.excerpt: Apple’s smaller Pro iPhone gets the best kind of spec bump for 2026: longer battery life, faster chips and a fancy new variable aperture for the main camera. The iPhone 18 Pro is one of a pair of slab phones launched alongside Apple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, and is the cheapest of the new phones, with a regular iPhone 18 yet to be announced. It isn’t exactly low cost, priced from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099), with a £100 or equivalent rise over previous models courtesy of RAMageddon. Having fully revamped the design of the body for the iPhone 17 Pro, the new model is a modest refinement. It is 7g heavier and the back glass now matches the colour of the aluminium body, which is available in a handful of new shades. Apple has shrunk the amount of the screen taken up by the Face ID camera, allowing the dynamic island to show three continuing tasks, up from two on previous devices. It also now shows the 3/4/5G indicator next to the signal level when playing music, which is a most appreciated feature for public transport commuters sorely missed on previous models. Otherwise, the 6.3in screen is one of the very best on a phone: super bright, crisp and smooth, while being big enough without making the phone enormous. An anti-glare coating makes it much easier to see outside, too.
/technology/2026/nov/06/struggling-to-sp.trail: Longer battery life, better screen, upgraded Siri and new variable aperture camera in refreshed design from last year’s model

/technology/2026/nov/06/struggling-to-sp.headline: ‘RAMageddon’: tech crunch hikes the price of your next iPhone by £100
/technology/2026/nov/06/struggling-to-sp.excerpt: Apple’s recent product launch caused headlines around the world as it unveiled its first folding phone. But hidden in the slick technology showcase was a nasty surprise: a £100 increase in the price of all iPhones, including older models. It is blamed on “RAMageddon”, which has reversed a decades-long trend of electronics becoming cheaper. It is the fallout from the AI gold rush hoovering up every memory chip available for vast datacentres. This has led to a severe shortage of the chips and other critical components for electronics, including phones. The situation has dramatically driven up costs, with some chips five times dearer than previously listed. Therefore the everyday electronics products people rely on are suddenly significantly more expensive to make, and that is being passed on to consumers. “Two things are happening at once,” says Francisco Jeronimo, the vice-president of client devices at research company IDC. “Component costs have risen sharply, with memory alone up more than 300% year on year.” Because older iPhones use the same expensive memory as the new ones, Apple is pricing them as current products, he adds. The iPhone is not the first product to have a RAMageddon price increase, but it is the single biggest-selling electrical product in the world. For many, this means the real cost of the AI splurge will be £100 without getting anything more for your money.
/technology/2026/nov/06/struggling-to-sp.trail: Shortage of memory chips and other critical components reverses trend of electronics becoming cheaper

/technology/2026/nov/06/struggling-to-sp.headline: The best iPhones: which Apple smartphone is right for you, according to our expert
/technology/2026/nov/06/struggling-to-sp.excerpt: The best iPhone may be the one you already own. There’s generally no need to buy a fresh phone just because new models have been released, as hardware updates are broadly iterative, adding small bits to an already accomplished package. But if you do want a replacement handset, whether new or refurbished, here are the best devices of the current crop of Apple smartphones. Many other smartphones are available besides the iPhone, but if you’re an Apple user and don’t fancy switching to Android, there are still a few choices to make. Whether your priority is the longest battery life, the best camera, the biggest screen or simply the optimal balance of features and price, there’s more to choose from in the Apple ecosystem than you may expect. Apple recently announced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, which are direct replacements for the previous Pro models and will be available from 18 September. They feature faster chips and a variable-aperture main camera for more creative photography options. It also unveiled its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, which adopts a squat, passport-like shape with a 5.4in screen on the outside and a 7.6in tablet screen on the inside when you open it like a book. The iPhone Duo will be available from 23 September. It did not announce a regular iPhone 18, leaving the iPhone 17 as Apple’s standard model for now.
